title: Cloud provider selection and due diligence
status_rationale: No cloud provider has been selected for Unbound; no selection criteria or due diligence record was located.
target_answer: Echelon selects Unbound's cloud provider through a recorded decision that compares candidates on: current SOC 1 and SOC 2 Type 2 reports and ISO/IEC 27001, 27017 and 27018 certificates covering the specific services used; availability of FIPS 140-3 validated key management; US regions with at least two availability zones for managed PostgreSQL 16 (Strata constraint); private networking for managed services; workload identity; data residency controls; financial stability; and exit feasibility. The decision, the provider's reports and the gaps found are retained and refreshed annually.
current_practice: Unknown; no evidence located. Hosting provider, regions and managed services for Unbound are not selected (no verified production infrastructure exists as of 2026-11-25).
intended_practice: Write the provider selection ADR with explicit criteria before any production resource is created.
customer_statement: Unbound's cloud provider has not yet been selected. Echelon can describe its selection criteria once documented but cannot name a provider today.
open_questions: Which cloud provider will host Unbound, and what criteria will decide it?
Is any target customer contractually restricted to particular providers (for example a bank that has already approved specific providers)?

title: Review of the cloud provider's assurance reports
status_rationale: SOC2-013 and SOC2-022 require inventory and review of subservice organizations; no provider and no review exist.
target_answer: Each year, and on each new report or bridge letter, Echelon obtains the provider's SOC 1 Type 2 (where the provider's services affect sponsors' financial reporting) and SOC 2 Type 2 reports, confirms the services Unbound uses are in scope, reviews exceptions and qualified opinions, and maps every complementary user entity control in the provider's report to an Echelon control with evidence. Gaps between report periods are covered by bridge letters. The review record is available to customers under NDA together with instructions for obtaining the provider's reports directly.
intended_practice: Create the CUEC mapping template now; complete it when the provider is selected.
customer_statement: Echelon plans to review its cloud provider's SOC reports annually and map the provider's complementary user entity controls to its own controls. No provider is selected yet.
residual_risks: Provider reports are carve-out style for their own subservice organizations; fourth-party coverage is partial.

title: Shared responsibility model
status_rationale: No responsibility matrix exists; Unbound also has a third party in the model (the sponsor), which requirements address in CNV-PAY-001 and the SOC 2 directive (SOC2-022).
target_answer: Echelon publishes a three-way responsibility matrix (cloud provider, Echelon, sponsor customer) for every control family: physical, network, host, platform, application, identity, data, keys, backups, incident response, and payment origination (the sponsor originates payments; Unbound is a third-party service provider per CNV-PAY-001). Each Echelon row links to an ECTL control and evidence requirement; each sponsor row is a complementary user entity control in Echelon's future SOC 2 report. The matrix is generated from the control register so it cannot drift from the controls actually implemented.
intended_practice: Draft the matrix structure in the control register; populate provider rows from the chosen provider's documentation.
customer_statement: A responsibility matrix covering Echelon, its cloud provider and customers is planned and will be shared once the provider is selected.
open_questions: Which security responsibilities will sponsors contractually retain (for example their own user administration and payment approvals)?

title: Subservice organizations in the SOC 2 report: carve-out versus inclusive method
status_rationale: No SOC 2 engagement exists; SOC2-022 requires defining CUECs and subservice organization controls; method not chosen.
target_answer: Echelon's SOC 2 report will use the carve-out method for its cloud provider and other infrastructure subservice organizations, which is standard practice because hyperscale providers do not participate in customers' audits. The report will list each carved-out subservice organization, the services it provides, and the complementary subservice organization controls (CSOCs) Echelon relies on, and Echelon will monitor those organizations through their own reports (ANS-CLD-002). Inclusive treatment would only be considered for a smaller subservice organization that agrees to it and whose controls are central to a customer commitment.
current_practice: Not established. No SOC 2 audit has been engaged.
intended_practice: Choose method with the auditor during readiness; document CSOCs from the provider's report.
customer_statement: Echelon has no SOC 2 report. When it obtains one, it expects to use the carve-out method for its cloud provider and to identify the provider controls it relies on.
open_questions: Which auditor will perform Echelon's SOC 2 and what is the planned first period?

challenge.customer_intent: Customers want the vendor's SOC 2 to cover everything that protects their data, including the hosting provider.
challenge.adverse_outcome: A control failure at the cloud provider that no report covers.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Inclusive reports give one opinion over both parties but are rarely obtainable from hyperscale providers; carve-out reports shift review work to the customer.
challenge.legally_required: No. SSAE 18 and the AICPA SOC 2 guide permit either method.
challenge.contractually_required: Some customer contracts ask for the vendor's SOC 2 to 'cover all subservice organizations', which customers often read as inclusive.
challenge.historical_convention: Carve-out is the norm for cloud-hosted SaaS.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Not applicable; this is an assurance-scope choice, not a control that architecture can remove.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Monitoring of provider reports and CSOC mapping can be tracked as recurring control tasks.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Provider configuration evidence (guardrails, CSPM, encryption state) is continuous and complements the provider's SOC report.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Carve-out plus continuous evidence of Echelon's configuration of provider services.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes, through the provider's report, the CSOC mapping, and Echelon's configuration evidence.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If a critical subservice organization has no SOC report at all, carve-out leaves an uncovered gap.
challenge.conventional_cost: Inclusive: usually not available at any price from hyperscale providers.
challenge.alternative_cost: Carve-out: no added audit fee; annual review effort.
challenge.alternative_risks: Customers must obtain and read the provider's report themselves.
supporting_arguments: Matches market practice and is achievable.
Avoids implying assurance Echelon's auditor did not give.

agent judgment: customer acceptance likelihood 'Likely; carve-out for hyperscale providers is well understood by bank and insurer reviewers.'; institutional acceptance rating 'likely' (unvalidated, no cited source).
opposing_arguments: Some procurement teams score 'inclusive' higher without understanding feasibility.
Smaller subservice organizations (AI model providers, email services) may lack SOC reports, weakening carve-out coverage.

Institutional acceptance is unvalidated: no buyer, auditor, regulator or insurer evidence or cited source supports an acceptance rating (DD-VAL-ADV-001, DD-VAL-ADV-002). Treat any rating as agent judgment until target-customer conversations or a sourced document support it.

history.change: BL-021: set institutional_acceptance to unknown (prior 'likely' was unsourced agent judgment, kept in supporting_arguments) and added an unvalidated-acceptance note to opposing_arguments (OBJ-VRM-019, OBJ-SKEPTIC-014).

title: Cloud configuration security posture and guardrails
target_answer: Insecure cloud configurations are prevented rather than found: organization-level policies deny creation of public storage, unencrypted storage, resources in unapproved regions, long-lived access keys and disabling of audit logging. A cloud security posture assessment runs continuously against a benchmark (CIS for the chosen provider) across all accounts; findings are routed with severity-based targets and suppressions require approved, expiring exceptions. Combined with IaC review (ECTL-INF-005) and drift reconciliation (ECTL-INF-006), this gives three layers: prevent, review, detect.
intended_practice: Write organization guardrails before first workload; enable provider-native posture assessment at account creation.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: preventive cloud guardrails plus continuous configuration assessment. Not yet implemented.

challenge.customer_intent: Customers want assurance that cloud misconfiguration will not expose their data.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Public storage buckets, open databases or disabled logging exposing donor data.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Commercial CSPM tools detect misconfiguration after it exists and generate high alert volume; they are only as good as triage.
challenge.contractually_required: Questionnaires increasingly ask 'Do you use a CSPM tool?'
challenge.historical_convention: CSPM emerged after many cloud breaches traced to configuration errors.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Organization-level deny policies make the most damaging configurations impossible to create in scope.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Guardrails apply at the provider API, so even console or compromised-credential actions are blocked.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Guardrail policy exports and denied-action logs prove prevention, not just detection.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Preventive guardrails plus provider-native posture assessment, without necessarily buying a third-party CSPM.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes, by exporting guardrail policies and showing denied attempts.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If guardrails can be disabled by the same administrators they constrain without separate approval.
challenge.alternative_risks: Guardrails can block legitimate emergency actions; exceptions need a controlled path.
supporting_arguments: Prevention beats detection for high-impact misconfigurations.

agent judgment: customer acceptance likelihood 'Likely if the answer explains guardrails plus detection; uncertain if the questionnaire insists on a named third-party tool.'; institutional acceptance rating 'likely' (unvalidated, no cited source).
opposing_arguments: Provider-native tools may miss cross-account or identity-graph risks that specialized CSPM finds.
Reviewers may prefer an independent tool over provider tooling.

Institutional acceptance is unvalidated: no buyer, auditor, regulator or insurer evidence or cited source supports an acceptance rating (DD-VAL-ADV-001, DD-VAL-ADV-002). Treat any rating as agent judgment until target-customer conversations or a sourced document support it.

title: Region selection and data residency
status_rationale: UNB-TEN-008 requires per-partner residency support where technically and legally applicable; no regions are chosen.
target_answer: All Unbound customer data, including backups, replicas, logs, search indexes, AI embeddings and caches, is stored and processed in United States regions only, enforced by an organization policy that denies resource creation elsewhere. A data location inventory lists every store and its region, including subservice organizations (email delivery, AI model providers, support tooling) and where their processing occurs. Support access from outside the United States is not permitted without customer agreement. If a sponsor requires a narrower residency (for example a specific region), its deployment cell is placed accordingly (UNB-TEN-008). Disaster recovery uses a second US region.
current_practice: Not established. Hosting provider, regions and managed services for Unbound are not selected (no verified production infrastructure exists as of 2026-11-25).
intended_practice: Decide region pair with the provider; enforce region allowlist by policy; inventory subprocessors' processing locations.
customer_statement: Planned: all customer data stored and processed in the United States, enforced by technical policy. Regions are not yet selected.
residual_risks: AI model providers and support tools may process data in other regions unless contractually restricted.
Some global providers' control planes and support staff operate outside the US even when data is stored in US regions.
open_questions: Which primary and recovery regions will be used?
Will any sponsor or donor population require non-US residency (for example EU donors under GDPR), and is Unbound expected to support it?
Where do candidate AI model providers process prompts and outputs?

title: Cloud account structure and root credential protection
target_answer: The cloud organization has separate accounts for production, non-production, security logging, shared build infrastructure and break-glass, with dedicated-infrastructure sponsors in their own production accounts (isolation profile C). Root or owner credentials for the organization and each account are protected with hardware-backed MFA, held under two-person control, never used for daily work, and every use alerts the security owner. Human access is federated from the workforce IdP with no local users; workloads use platform-issued identities with no long-lived access keys. Security logging is written to an account that production administrators cannot modify.
intended_practice: Create account structure as the first IaC module.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: separate cloud accounts for production, non-production and security logging, with root credentials under two-person hardware-MFA control. Not yet implemented.
open_questions: Who will hold cloud root credentials and the second share at launch?

title: Cloud concentration risk and exit strategy
status_rationale: Exit requirements exist for sponsors leaving Unbound (RR-UNB-TEN-016-r1) but not for Echelon leaving its provider; nothing is implemented.
target_answer: Unbound accepts single-provider concentration deliberately and manages it rather than running multi-cloud. Mitigations: the application is one portable .NET deployable in a standard container; the authoritative store is PostgreSQL (portable engine), managed by Strata's declarative schemas; infrastructure is codified; backups are exported in a provider-neutral format to storage under separate credentials; and an exit runbook is tested annually by restoring a representative tenant into an alternate environment and verifying ledger integrity. Provider-specific services (KMS, identity) are isolated behind adapters. Echelon discloses the provider concentration to customers so they can assess their own aggregate exposure.
intended_practice: Write exit runbook with the hosting decision; schedule first restore-elsewhere test before general availability.
customer_statement: Planned: Unbound will run on a single cloud provider with a documented and periodically tested exit plan. Not yet implemented.
residual_risks: A provider-wide outage or account suspension would stop Unbound until recovery elsewhere; recovery time for an exit is unmeasured.
Keys held in a provider KMS cannot be exported; exit requires decrypt-and-re-encrypt or a key hierarchy that supports migration.
open_questions: What recovery time objective applies to a forced provider exit, and will sponsors accept it?

challenge.customer_intent: Banks and regulators want assurance that failure of one cloud provider will not halt critical services, and that many institutions are not all exposed to the same provider.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Extended outage or forced exit from the provider stopping grants and payments.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Active multi-cloud doubles operational complexity, lowers the security baseline in each cloud, and is rarely tested end to end; it often adds risk.
challenge.legally_required: Not for Echelon directly. EU DORA imposes concentration risk assessment on EU financial entities, which does not apply to US DAF sponsors. US interagency TPRM guidance expects banks to consider concentration risk, which may flow to vendors contractually.
challenge.contractually_required: Some bank contracts ask for an exit plan; few require multi-cloud.
challenge.historical_convention: Multi-data-center redundancy was the norm before regional cloud availability zones.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Portable components (container, PostgreSQL, IaC) remove most lock-in at the application layer.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Backups in provider-neutral format are produced automatically.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Annual restore-elsewhere test results show exit is feasible and measure the time.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Single provider, multi-zone and multi-region, with tested portability.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If provider-specific services become embedded in the core without adapters.
challenge.conventional_cost: Multi-cloud: very high build and recurring cost.
challenge.alternative_cost: Tested exit plan: medium build, low recurring.
challenge.alternative_risks: Exit test may not reflect a real emergency where the provider is unavailable for data export.
supporting_arguments: Exit testing is verifiable; multi-cloud claims often are not.

agent judgment: customer acceptance likelihood 'Likely for most customers; uncertain for large banks with concentration policies.'; institutional acceptance rating 'uncertain' (unvalidated, no cited source).
opposing_arguments: Concentration remains; a long provider outage is not mitigated by an exit plan that takes weeks.
Regulators may view single-provider dependence of critical financial services skeptically.

Institutional acceptance is unvalidated: no buyer, auditor, regulator or insurer evidence or cited source supports an acceptance rating (DD-VAL-ADV-001, DD-VAL-ADV-002). Treat any rating as agent judgment until target-customer conversations or a sourced document support it.

title: Managed services and other subservice organizations inventory
status_rationale: SOC2-013 requires inventory of critical services and subservice organizations; none exist yet. Unbound requirements name several categories (payment providers, custodians, charity data, AI models, telephony).
target_answer: Echelon maintains a register of every managed cloud service and external provider that stores, processes or can access customer data, generated from the provider adapter registry and IaC: service, provider, data classes, region, whether it is a subservice organization for SOC 2 purposes, its assurance report status, contractual terms, and the CSOCs relied upon. The register drives the customer-facing subprocessor list and SOC 2 system description, and adding a provider requires a security and privacy design review (SOC2-030).
intended_practice: Create the register schema in the control register; populate from provider adapters as they are designed.
customer_statement: Planned: a maintained inventory of all managed services and subprocessors with their assurance status, published to customers. Not yet available.
open_questions: Which managed services (KMS, email, AI models, observability) will be subservice organizations versus vendors outside the system boundary?
